title: Change control & configuration management defined
blurb: Define change control and configuration management, and tell them apart in any scenario.
question: On a library refurbishment, one builder fits shelving from an out-of-date drawing while a trustee asks for a café to be added. Which discipline keeps everyone on the right drawing, and which decides whether the café goes ahead?

teach.body: Once the scope is agreed and baselined, two disciplines protect it. Change control decides whether a proposed change to that baseline is allowed. Configuration management keeps track of the things the project is producing: what each item is, which version is current and what has changed. One guards the door; the other keeps the inventory. You need both to stop scope creep, the uncontrolled growth of scope.

Formally: the administrative activities concerned with the creation, maintenance, controlled change and quality control of the scope of work. In plain English: you know exactly what you are building, every item has a name and a version, only controlled changes are made to it, and you can prove the item is right. Those items are called configuration items.

teach.caption: Every configuration item carries a unique reference and a version, so revision D can never be confused with revision B.

teach.body: Formally: the process through which all requests to change the approved baseline of a project are captured, evaluated and then approved, rejected or deferred. In plain English: nobody changes what was agreed on a whim. Every request is written down, its impact is weighed up, and someone with the authority makes a clear decision before any work starts.

teach.h: Every request ends in one of three decisions
teach.caption: Riverside example: a trustee's request for a café is captured and evaluated, then approved, rejected or deferred.
Different jobs, same aim: a scope that only changes in a controlled, recorded way.

teach.body: Change control only bites once there is an approved baseline to protect. Before that, scope is still being defined. After it, every request is measured against the baseline, and configuration management records each item at its baselined version. If either is missing, small unrecorded tweaks pile up into scope creep: more cost, more time and products nobody signed off.

teach.text: Don't swap the jobs: configuration management does not approve changes, and change control does not keep version records. And change control is not 'change management', which is about helping people and organisations adopt change.

items: Configuration management: the administrative activities for the creation, maintenance, controlled change and quality control of the scope of work.
Configuration items: products, components, documents and their versions.
Change control: requests to change the approved baseline are captured, evaluated, then approved, rejected or deferred.
Change control decides whether; configuration management records what and which version.

summary: You can now define configuration management and change control in close-to-APM wording and in plain English. You can also spot which discipline a scenario describes and name the three possible change decisions.

A.q: Which of the following best describes change control?
options: Recording which version of each product is current
Managing the people side of organisational change
Capturing, evaluating and deciding on baseline changes
Checking finished products meet their specification
A.why: Change control is the process through which requests to change the approved baseline are captured, evaluated and then approved, rejected or deferred.

whyNot.0: Recording the current version of each item is configuration management.
whyNot.1: Helping people adopt change is change management, a different discipline.
whyNot.3: Checking products against their specification is a quality control activity.

A.q: Complete the statement: configuration management covers the administrative activities concerned with the creation, maintenance, controlled change and quality control of the…
A.why: Configuration management controls the scope of work: the configuration items the project creates and maintains.

whyNot.1: The budget is managed through cost control, not configuration management.
whyNot.2: The risk register is managed through risk management.
whyNot.3: A stakeholder map supports stakeholder engagement, not configuration management.

A.q: Which of these would be placed under configuration management on the Riverside Library refurbishment?
options: An informal chat about paint colours
A.why: An approved drawing is a configuration item: it needs a unique reference, a version and controlled change.

whyNot.0: An informal conversation is not a product, component or controlled document.
whyNot.1: A sales brochure is not something the project produces or baselines.
whyNot.2: Personal notes are not project deliverables, so they are not controlled items.

B.q: Which three outcomes can a change control decision lead to?
B.why: Every request to change the baseline ends in one of three decisions: approved, rejected or deferred.

whyNot.0: Escalating or closing are not the defined outcomes of a change decision.
whyNot.2: Accept, transfer and reduce are risk responses, not change decisions.
whyNot.3: Raising and recording happen before the decision; they are not outcomes.

B.q: Change control is applied to requests to change which of the following?
B.why: Change control exists to protect the approved baseline: every request to change it is captured and evaluated.

whyNot.0: An informal ideas list has not been baselined, so there is nothing to control yet.
whyNot.1: Organisational strategy is set above the project, not through project change control.
whyNot.2: Roles are set through governance and the organisation, not through change requests.

B.q: Which statement about configuration management is correct?
options: It controls products and their versions
It decides whether changes are approved
It applies only to software deliverables
It replaces the need for change control
B.why: Configuration management identifies the project's items and controls their versions and changes.

whyNot.1: Deciding on changes is the job of change control.
whyNot.2: It applies to any product, component or document: drawings, specs, hardware and software alike.
whyNot.3: The two work together; configuration management depends on change control to authorise changes.

C.q: Riverside's trustees ask to swap the approved carpet for wooden flooring. Which discipline decides whether this goes ahead?
C.why: A request to alter the approved baseline is captured, evaluated and decided through change control.

whyNot.0: Configuration management records the items and versions; it does not make the decision.
whyNot.1: Quality assurance gives confidence the project will meet its quality requirements; it does not decide on changes.
whyNot.3: Benefits management tracks and realises benefits; it does not decide on scope changes.

C.q: Riverside's PM keeps a register giving every drawing a reference, a version number and an approval status. Which discipline is she applying?
C.why: Uniquely referencing items and recording their version and status is configuration management.

whyNot.0: Change control decides on requests; it does not maintain the version register.
whyNot.2: Requirements management captures what stakeholders need; it does not track versions of each drawing.
whyNot.3: Stakeholder management deals with people's interests and influence, not version records.

C.q: Which TWO statements are true? 1. A change request can be deferred. 2. Configuration management starts only at handover. 3. Configuration items include documents. 4. Change control applies before any baseline exists.
C.why: Requests can be approved, rejected or deferred (1), and configuration items include products, components and documents (3).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is false: configuration management runs throughout the project, not just at handover.
whyNot.2: Both are false: configuration management is continuous, and change control protects an approved baseline.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: change control applies to changes to an approved baseline.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: You are having a kitchen extension built. Who keeps track of the drawings, and who agrees any change to them?

blocks.body: The architect keeps a drawing register: each drawing has a number and a revision letter, and the builder must work from the latest approved one. That is configuration management. Halfway through, you ask for a bigger window. The builder cannot just do it: you agree a written variation after seeing the extra cost and delay. That is change control. The register tells you which drawing to change; the variation decides whether to change it.

blocks.text: The architect's register never approves the bigger window, and the variation never tells the builder which drawing revision is current. Two jobs, two disciplines.

explain.body: The administrative activities for the creation, maintenance, controlled change and quality control of the scope of work. Put simply: everyone works from the right version of each item, and you can prove it.

test.q: In plain English, configuration management makes sure that everyone:
options: uses the right version of every item
knows who approves the project budget
follows the same risk management plan
test.why: Its purpose is control of the scope of work: every item identified, versioned and correct.

whyNot.0: Agreeing the business case is part of governance and sponsorship.
whyNot.2: Budget approval sits with the sponsor and governance, not configuration management.
whyNot.3: Following the risk management plan is part of risk management.

explain.body: The things under configuration management: products, the components that make them up, and the documents that describe them, each with its version. If the project produces it and others rely on it, it is a candidate.

rows: No: not a product or document

test.q: Which of the following is NOT typically a configuration item?
test.why: A passing comment is not a product, component or controlled document, so it is not a configuration item.

whyNot.0: A signed specification is a controlled document: a configuration item.
whyNot.1: A software component is part of a product: a configuration item.
whyNot.2: A versioned user guide is a controlled document: a configuration item.

explain.body: The process through which all requests to change the approved baseline are captured, evaluated and then approved, rejected or deferred. Nothing changes until someone with authority has decided.

steps.label: Captured
steps.sub: The request is written down and logged

test.q: Complete the statement: change control is the process through which all requests to change the approved baseline are captured, evaluated and then…
test.why: After capture and evaluation, every request is approved, rejected or deferred.

whyNot.0: Implementation only follows if the request is approved; some are rejected or deferred.
whyNot.1: The lessons log captures learning, not change decisions.
whyNot.3: Escalation is not the defined end point; the request must be approved, rejected or deferred.

explain.body: Once the baseline is approved, small unrecorded changes add up to scope creep: uncontrolled growth in scope, with extra cost and time nobody agreed. Change control stops this without banning change: good changes can still be approved.

test.q: Why does a project need change control once its baseline is agreed?
options: To stop all changes to the scope
To remove the need for a sponsor
test.why: Change control makes sure changes are evaluated and authorised, preventing uncontrolled growth in scope.

whyNot.0: Change control does not stop change: requests can be approved.
whyNot.1: The sponsor, or another appropriate authority, is the one who decides on change requests.
whyNot.2: An approved change can alter the budget; nothing is frozen forever.
